A bibliography is a list of written sources — such as books, articles, journals, or websites — connected either to a specific piece of writing or to a specific subject. The word always revolves around the same idea: a structured, organized record of written works.

The word has four distinct but related uses. Understanding all four will give you complete command of it.

1. The list of sources at the end of a document (most common)

When a writer — a student, researcher, or author — writes an essay, research paper, or book, they often draw information from other sources. A bibliography is the formal list of all those sources, placed at the very end of the document. Think of it as a receipt of all the information the writer "borrowed" or consulted.

Each item on this list is called a bibliographic entry, and it tells the reader exactly where a piece of information came from. A typical entry includes the author's name, the title of the work, the publisher, the year of publication, and — for websites — the web address and the date it was accessed.

2. A standalone list of writings on a particular subject

A bibliography can also exist as its own independent document, not attached to any essay or book. For example, "A Bibliography of the French Revolution" would be a collection listing every significant book, paper, and article ever written about the French Revolution. Scholars, librarians, and researchers create these to help others find everything available on a given topic in one place.

3. A complete list of works by a single author

The word can also refer to all the works produced by one specific writer. If someone says "the bibliography of Virginia Woolf," they mean a full, organized list of everything Woolf ever wrote — her novels, essays, letters, diary entries, and so on.

4. The academic study of books (most specialized)

At its most scholarly level, bibliography is the name of an entire academic discipline — the systematic study of books as physical objects. This field examines things like: how books were printed, what paper and ink were used, how different editions of the same book differ from one another, how errors crept into texts over centuries, and how books are formally described and classified. A person who specializes in this field is called a bibliographer.

Giving credit where it's due. A bibliography acknowledges the original authors whose ideas or research a writer used. Without this acknowledgment, using someone else's work is called plagiarism — a serious academic and ethical offense.

Letting readers verify information. A bibliography allows readers to go back to the original sources themselves, check whether the information is accurate, and read further if they wish.

Showing the quality of research. A thorough, well-constructed bibliography signals that a writer did serious, careful research rather than relying on guesswork or memory.
Bibliography vs. Works Cited vs. References

These three terms are commonly confused, so it's worth clarifying them precisely:

A bibliography lists every source a writer consulted during their research — including sources they read for background understanding but may not have directly mentioned in the text.

A Works Cited page lists only the sources the writer actually cited (quoted or referenced) within the text itself. Nothing more, nothing less. This term is standard in MLA format, commonly used in literature and language studies.

A References page works similarly to a Works Cited page — only directly cited sources — and is the standard term used in APA format, common in psychology, education, and the social sciences.

In everyday conversation, people often use all three terms interchangeably, but in academic writing, the distinction matters.

Bibliographies follow specific formatting rules that vary by field and institution. The four most widely used styles are APA (American Psychological Association), MLA (Modern Language Association), Chicago Style, and Harvard referencing. Each has its own rules about the order of information, punctuation, capitalization, and indentation within an entry. The content of each entry is largely the same — author, title, publisher, date — but the way it's presented differs.

Bibliography, as a noun, most commonly means the list of sources found at the end of a piece of writing. More broadly, it can mean a standalone, curated list of all writings on a particular subject or by a particular author. At its most technical, it refers to the scholarly discipline devoted to the study of books as physical and historical objects. In all its uses, the word is fundamentally about tracking, organizing, and presenting information about written works in a clear and accountable way.
